newsitem.title: USA: TWA Q4 loss puts strategy under spotlight.
newsitem.headline: TWA Q4 loss puts strategy under spotlight.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc on Tuesday reported a wider-than-expected net loss for the fourth quarter, raising questions about whether its latest strategy can address its problems quickly enough, analysts said.
"The loss was wider than expected," Goldman Sachs analyst Glenn Engel said. "It was disappointing on the top line as well as in operations."
"They're in a pretty big hole, but the question is are they moving fast enough (to fix the problems)?," Engel added.

Earlier Tuesday, the nation's seventh largest air carrier reported a loss of $258.6 million in the fourth quarter ended December 31, or $5.56 a share, compared to a loss of $27.8 million or $0.84 a share a year ago.

TWA said the current quarter included charges of $85.9 million related to the planned retirement of certain jet fleets, higher overseas severance costs and a writedown of the carrying value of its New York-Athens route authority, which is scheduled to be terminated after April 18.
The carrier said it is taking actions to revive its restructuring plan, which stalled in 1996.

The moves include a new flight schedule using available aircraft and personnel, replacing older jets with more efficient planes, refining the route system and launching a new plan at John F. Kennedy Airport in New York and at Lambert-St. Louis International Airport, TWA said.
"Last year's strategy was to add flights and aggressively expand in markets where there was less business," Engel said. "(Now) it seems like they're moving in the right direction."
Engel pointed out that TWA was moving away from plans in 1996 to use larger planes he said were more difficult to fill as well as to operate.
He also said the fact TWA lost a total of $284.8 million or $7.27 a share in 1997, a year where the airline industry posted record profits, was not a good sign.
Analyst Stephen Klein of S&P Equity Group added TWA is lucky 1997 is expected to be another good year for airlines.
"The problem is what will happen (to TWA) in a bad year?," he asked.
Klein said he was also surprised the company did not hold a conference call with analysts to discuss its new programs.
"The company is in trouble and (TWA officials) could have elaborated on a concrete turnaround plan," he said.
A TWA spokesman confirmed no conference call was scheduled and he declined to comment on specific marketing plans TWA said it was considering for business travelers.
Klein predicted TWA will lose money in 1997, about $0.15 a share, but not as much as it did in 1996.
The TWA spokesman said the company does not project future earnings.
TWA shares were trading off 7/16 Tuesday at 6-7/8.
